title.en: Analyse the voltage divider bias circuit
Explain the role of the emitter resistor

say.en: Open almost any discrete transistor amplifier and you will find four resistors around the transistor. This is voltage divider bias, and it barely cares what beta is. In this lesson: Analyse the voltage divider bias circuit.
Explain the role of the emitter resistor.

body.en: Resistors $R_1$ and $R_2$ form a divider across $V_{CC}$ and fix the base *voltage* $V_B = V_{CC} R_2/(R_1+R_2)$ (when the divider current is much larger than $I_B$). The emitter voltage is $V_E = V_B - V_{BE}$, so $I_E = V_E/R_E$ and $I_C \approx I_E$. Finally $V_{CE} \approx V_{CC} - I_C (R_C + R_E)$.

narration.en: The divider fixes the base voltage. Subtract V B E to get the emitter voltage, divide by R E for the current, and beta does not appear anywhere.
narration.kn: ವಿಭಾಜಕವು ಬೇಸ್ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ಅನ್ನು ಸ್ಥಿರಗೊಳಿಸುತ್ತದೆ. Vbe ಕಳೆದರೆ ಎಮಿಟರ್ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್; Re ಯಿಂದ ಭಾಗಿಸಿದರೆ ಪ್ರವಾಹ. ಬೀಟಾ ಎಲ್ಲಿಯೂ ಬರುವುದಿಲ್ಲ.

say.en: The divider fixes the base voltage. Subtract V B E to get the emitter voltage, divide by R E for the current, and beta does not appear anywhere. V B equals V CC R2/R1 plus R2.

say.en: I E equals (V B - V BE)/R E is approximately I C.
V CE is approximately V CC - I C R C plus R E.

title.en: On the board: Voltage divider bias

say.en: Two resistors R1 and R2 divide VCC to fix the base voltage. An emitter resistor RE is added.
The divider fixes VB. The emitter is one VBE below it, so IE is set by RE. Beta does not appear at all.
Example: 12 volts, R1 50 kilo-ohms, R2 10 kilo-ohms, RE 1.3 kilo-ohms, RC 4.7 kilo-ohms. VB is 2 volts, IE 1 milliampere, VCE 6 volts.
If IC tries to rise, VE rises; with VB fixed, VBE falls and pulls IC back. This gives S close to 1, the best of all.
On the board: Voltage divider bias.

narration.en: R1 and R2 fix the base voltage, so the emitter voltage VE = VB − 0.7 and IE = VE/RE hardly depend on β. If IC rises, the drop across RE rises and VBE falls, pulling IC back. VCC = 12 V and RC = 2 kΩ.
narration.kn: R1, R2 ಆಧಾರ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ನಿಗದಿ ಮಾಡುತ್ತವೆ; VE = VB − 0.7, IE = VE/RE, β ಮೇಲೆ ಅಷ್ಟು ಅವಲಂಬಿಸುವುದಿಲ್ಲ. IC ಏರಿದರೆ RE ಮೇಲಿನ ಇಳಿಕೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿ VBE ಕಡಿಮೆಯಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

body.en: If $I_C$ tends to rise, $V_E = I_E R_E$ rises. Since $V_B$ is fixed by the divider, $V_{BE} = V_B - V_E$ falls, reducing $I_B$ and pulling $I_C$ back. This *emitter* (negative) feedback gives a stability factor close to 1. A bypass capacitor across $R_E$ removes this feedback for ac signals so that the gain is not lost.

points.en: Bypass capacitor C_E keeps ac gain high

narration.en: The emitter resistor gives negative feedback: a rise in current raises V E, which lowers V B E and brings the current back down.
narration.kn: ಎಮಿಟರ್ ರೆಸಿಸ್ಟರ್ ಋಣಾತ್ಮಕ ಪ್ರತಿಪೋಷಣೆ ನೀಡುತ್ತದೆ: ಪ್ರವಾಹ ಏರಿದರೆ Ve ಏರುತ್ತದೆ, Vbe ಇಳಿಯುತ್ತದೆ ಮತ್ತು ಪ್ರವಾಹ ಮತ್ತೆ ಕಡಿಮೆಯಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

say.en: The emitter resistor gives negative feedback: a rise in current raises V E, which lowers V B E and brings the current back down. I C ↑ gives V E ↑ gives V BE ↓ gives I B ↓ gives I C ↓.

tagline.en: How negative feedback stabilises the Q-point, the collector-to-base bias circuit, the voltage divider (self) bias circuit with its approximate and Thevenin analysis, and a comparison of stability factors.

myth.en: In voltage divider bias, V_CE = V_CC − I_C R_C, the same as in fixed bias.

truth.en: With an emitter resistor, V_CE = V_CC − I_C(R_C + R_E), taking I_C ≈ I_E. The collector current flows through both R_C and R_E, so both drops must be subtracted. The DC load line then ends at V_CC/(R_C + R_E) on the current axis.

say.en: Here $R_B$ is connected from the collector (not from $V_{CC}$) to the base. The current in $R_C$ is $I_C + I_B = (1 + \beta)I_B$.

Resistors $R_1$ (from $V_{CC}$ to base) and $R_2$ (from base to ground) form a potential divider that fixes the base voltage. An emitter resistor $R_E$ provides the feedback: if $I_C$ rises, $V_E = I_E R_E$ rises, so $V_{BE} = V_B - V_E$ falls and $I_B$ falls.

The collector current flows through both R_C and R_E, so both drops must be subtracted. The DC load line then ends at V_CC/(R_C + R_E) on the current axis.

problem.en: Voltage divider bias: V_CC = 15 V, R1 = 40 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_C = 3 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, V_BE = 0.7 V. Find the Q-point.

answer.en: Q-point = (5.8 V, 2.3 mA), independent of β

narration.en: Let us work this out together. Voltage divider bias: V_CC = 15 V, R1 = 40 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_C = 3 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, V_BE = 0.7 V. Find the Q-point.

say.en: Let us work this out together. Voltage divider bias: V CC equals 15 volts, R1 equals 40 k ohms, R2 equals 10 k ohms, R C equals 3 k ohms, R E equals 1 k ohms, V BE equals 0.7 volts. Find the Q-point.
V B equals 15 times 10 over 40 plus 10 equals 3 volts.
V E equals 3 minus 0.7 equals 2.3 volts; I E equals 2.3 V over 1 k ohms equals 2.3 milliamperes is approximately I C.
V CE equals 15 minus 2.3 milliamperes times 3 plus 1 k ohms equals 15 minus 9.2 equals 5.8 volts.
So the answer is Q-point equals (5.8 volts, 2.3 milliamperes), independent of beta.
